description: Hey, we’re NAISA! Five students from universities across Korea, united by a love of space, engineering, gaming, and learning. In two days, we turned question marks into shared “It works!” moments—and became a crew. We took on this hackathon to build a game that lets others experience the same joy of teamwork we found together. Our mission: help players tackle a space mission, discover the power of collaboration, and celebrate what they can achieve as a team. Jump aboard and shout: “WE did that!”
summary:
Project NAISA is a cooperative strategy game that lets players experience the challenge of designing and managing a complete space mission together. In aerospace missions, each subsystem may work as intended on its own, yet the mission can still run into problems if the parts do not work well together or their combined demands exceed shared limits such as budget, mass, power, time, and data. In the NOVA-1 mission to investigate possible subsurface water ice on Mars, four players take on different roles and make interdependent decisions across a series of games. They experience how choices in one area affect the rest of the mission and work together to balance limited resources and achieve their objective. As players work through these decisions, a friendly guide character, Ni-SAR-1114, introduces key concepts and leads them through the experience.

By turning these trade-offs into play, Project NAISA makes systems engineering easier to explore and understand. Although NOVA-1 is fictional, the game draws on NASA’s exploration history and mission data, while equipment values are simplified for educational purposes. This allows players to focus on how design choices affect the mission. Ultimately, the game shows that mission success depends on effective teamwork and well-integrated systems.
details:
KEYWORDS

Cooperative Experience / Interactive Gameplay / System Engineering / Spacecraft Configuration / Mission Planning / Mars Exploration

THE STORY SO FAR

The late 2040s. A flag rises over the red horizon, and a broadcast reaches Earth: the Severian Federation has landed the first humans on Mars. Inside NAISA’s mission control, silence falls. Years of preparation for NOVA-1—and someone else has taken the first footsteps. Then a new order arrives: 

“Proceed to Sector A-17. Gather the evidence. Bring everyone home.”

The mission has changed. What your team brings back could help shape the future of human exploration on Mars. With three explorers bound for the Red Planet and one teammate guiding them from Earth, every message matters. A solar storm threatens the journey ahead. The Martian surface holds unanswered questions. And even after the exploration is over, space debris stands between your crew and home. Can you work together to bring back answers—and make it home safely?

GEAR UP. LAUNCH. EXPLORE.

Cooperative Mission Design

Four players take on different roles to design a Mars exploration spacecraft together. Since each piece of equipment has its own cost, mass, and performance, the team must find a configuration that fits the mission while staying within limited resources. This stage introduces players to the trade-offs involved in systems engineering. For example, a heavier spacecraft requires greater thrust, while improving performance can increase costs or place additional demands on other resources. Players must consider resource limits, mission requirements, and the likelihood of completing the mission to find the best design for their circumstances—not simply choose the most powerful equipment.

  • Mission Coordinator: Reviews the full mission briefing, shares key information, and helps the team make decisions during the mission.
  • Spacecraft Engineer: Configures the spacecraft’s structure and propulsion systems, and considers how the design affects flight and landing.
  • Pilot: Selects the science and sample-preservation systems needed to collect, analyze, and protect subsurface ice samples on Mars. 
  • Avionics Engineer: Configures and manages communications and power systems to support the spacecraft’s safe and reliable operation.


Orbit Setting: Find the Efficient Path

In this stage, players plan a trajectory to Mars by adjusting the departure date, launch direction, and departure velocity change (ΔV). Different settings affect flight time, fuel use, and whether the spacecraft can reach Mars. Players must consider the spacecraft's propulsion capability and mission constraints to find a feasible route.

The trajectory simulation uses simplified orbital mechanics and planetary position data based on JPL DE421 ephemeris. Its trajectory-planning approach is informed by NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). This stage introduces players to how orbital mechanics influences mission planning. Rather than simply choosing the fastest route, players experiment with different conditions and compare the results to find a trajectory that best fits their spacecraft's capabilities and mission objectives.


MARSBOUND: Survive the Solar Storm!

You have 15 seconds to reach Mars—and a solar particle storm stands in your way! Coordinate your controls in real time, brace for a solar flare around the 10-second mark, and work together to get your crew safely through.

  • Mission Coordinator: Cuts high-voltage power when the solar flare hits, then restores it once the danger passes.
  • Spacecraft Engineer: Uses the number keys to release satellites and boost thrust. Keep an eye on your fuel—every boost counts!
  • Pilot: Uses the arrow keys to steer the spacecraft and keep Mars within your targeting zone.
  • Avionics Engineer: Switches gyroscope control at the right moment to keep the spacecraft’s orientation stable.

Mars Exploration

Four players, four roles, one shared mission: explore Mars and bring everyone home safely! Work together to choose your equipment, plan operations, and make the most of limited resources. Investigate possible underground ice in Mars’s A-17 sector and gather the evidence your team needs to turn questions into discoveries.

  • Mission Coordinator: Leads the briefing from mission control on Earth. Share keywords and critical updates to help your crew make informed decisions in the field.
  • Spacecraft Engineer: Configures the spacecraft’s propulsion, structure, and landing systems. Keep the craft and exploration equipment ready for safe operation.
  • Pilot: Takes the controls, chooses exploration sites and scientific instruments, and leads sample collection and analysis.
  • Avionics Engineer: Sets up and manages communications, power, and navigation systems. Keep the spacecraft running smoothly and exploration data flowing.

EARTHBOUND: Dodge the Debris!


Race back to Earth before time runs out! In this cooperative challenge, your crew must dodge space debris, manage boosts, and keep a sharp eye out for target objects along the way.

  • Spacecraft Engineer: Presses the number keys to release satellites and boost the spacecraft while managing fuel carefully.
  • Pilot: Uses the arrow keys to steer the spacecraft and dodge obstacles.
  • Mission Coordinator & Avionics Engineer: Watch for objects matching the keywords revealed at the start and count them as you fly. Enter the answers using the number keys after arrival—correct counts earn bonus points.

Earth Landing

Home is within reach—but there’s one final stage to complete. The return capsule descends toward Earth, using parachutes to slow its fall before splashing down in the ocean. A safe splashdown marks the entire crew’s successful return. After the journey to Mars and back, your crew can finally celebrate: everyone is home!

Mission Results & Feedback

The mission is over—time to see what your crew accomplished! Explore your final results and team score breakdown, celebrate the MVP and each player’s contributions and awards, and see where your team stands on the leaderboard. Look back on the decisions that shaped your journey and discover what you could do differently on your next mission.
